reading.title: The Map in the Wall
reading.text:
When the builders knocked down the wall of Grandpa Rashid’s old kitchen, a cloud of dust rolled out, and so did a rusty tin box.
Layla reached it first. Inside, wrapped in an oily cloth, was a map drawn in faded brown ink. It showed the village as it must have looked long ago: a cluster of houses, a well, three palm trees and, in the corner, a small cross marked with the words ‘Under the singing stone.’
“Treasure!” breathed her cousin Khalid.
Grandpa Rashid peered at the map through his glasses and laughed softly. “My father drew this,” he said. “He loved puzzles. But I have never heard a stone sing.”
For a whole week, Layla and Khalid searched. They tapped rocks, listened at walls and dug where the palm trees had once stood. They found bottle tops, a broken comb and a great many ants, but nothing that sang.
Then, one windy afternoon, Layla heard it: a low, hollow whistle coming from the edge of the old well. The wind was blowing across a hole in one of the stones. The stone was singing.
Behind it, sealed in clay, was a letter. Great-grandfather had written: ‘The real treasure is the time you spent looking together.’ Khalid groaned. Layla grinned.

reading.title: Why Do We Sleep?
reading.text:
Every night, your body switches into a different mode. You might think that nothing much happens while you sleep, but your brain and body are extremely busy.
During sleep, your brain sorts through everything you have learnt during the day. It decides which memories to keep and stores them, a bit like filing papers in the right folders. This is one reason why a good night’s sleep before a test can help you remember more.
Your body also uses sleep to repair itself. Muscles mend, cuts heal and, in children, special chemicals help the body to grow. Even your immune system, which fights germs, works harder while you rest.
Scientists recommend that children aged six to twelve get between nine and twelve hours of sleep each night. Screens can make this harder, because their light tricks the brain into thinking it is still daytime. That is why experts suggest switching off devices at least an hour before bed.

qs.a: Their light tricks the brain into thinking it is daytime.
c: Their light tricks the brain into thinking it is daytime.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of this text?
qs.a: to explain why sleep is important
c: to explain why sleep is important

reading.title: The Goalkeeper
reading.text:
Yusuf had always played in attack. He was the fastest runner in Grade 4 and he loved the moment when the ball hit the back of the net. So when Coach Amira told him he would be in goal for the final, he stared at her as if she had asked him to play in his pyjamas.
“But I’m a striker,” he protested.
“Our goalkeeper has a broken wrist,” Coach Amira said gently. “And you have the quickest reactions in the team.”
Yusuf spent the whole week sulking. He dived half-heartedly in training and let in goal after goal. His friends started to whisper.
The night before the final, his older sister found him sitting on the doorstep. “You know what makes a good goalkeeper?” she said. “Not hands. Courage. A goalkeeper is the last person standing between his team and defeat.”
The next afternoon, the score was 1–1 with a minute to go when the other team’s captain broke through. Yusuf did not think. He threw himself to the left, and his fingertips pushed the ball around the post.
As his teammates piled on top of him, Yusuf realised that saving a goal felt every bit as good as scoring one.

reading.title: Volcanoes
reading.text:
Deep beneath our feet, the Earth is incredibly hot. In some places, the rock is so hot that it melts into a thick liquid called magma. Because magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, it slowly rises towards the surface.
A volcano forms where magma finds a way out through a crack in the Earth’s crust. When magma reaches the surface, it is called lava. Lava can be hotter than 1,000 °C, which is about ten times hotter than boiling water.
Not all volcanoes erupt in the same way. Some ooze rivers of lava that move slowly downhill. Others explode violently, blasting clouds of ash and rock high into the sky. Volcanoes that have erupted recently are called active, while those that have not erupted for thousands of years are called dormant, which means sleeping.
Although volcanoes can be dangerous, they are also useful. Volcanic ash makes soil very rich, so farmers often grow crops on the slopes of old volcanoes.
